title: Grade XI Unit 3 — NBF textbook Numerical Exercises 3.1–3.8 (adapted & solved)
source: NBF Grade XI Physics, Unit 3, textbook pp. 51–52
policy: Six exercises are summative-aligned applications (B-04/05/12); 3.6 is formative B-11; 3.8 is supplementary formative/cross-topic. Suggested marking steps are teacher study guidance, NOT official FBISE marking scheme.

numericals.question: Compare the stopping distances of a car travelling at 30 m/s when its uniform deceleration is 7.00 m/s² on dry concrete and 5.00 m/s² on wet concrete.

steps.text: Use the constant-acceleration relation v² = u² + 2as and take the direction of travel as positive.
The wet-road stopping distance exceeds the dry-road distance by 25.7 m (about 40% longer).

numericals.answer: Dry: 64.3 m; wet: 90.0 m (wet is 25.7 m longer).
numericals.note: Assumes the stated decelerations are constant; does not include driver reaction distance.

numericals.question: For an ideal projectile launched and landing at the same level, find the projection angle at which its maximum height equals its horizontal range.
numericals.given: H = R; same launch and landing level; no air resistance; 0° < θ < 90°.

steps.text: For the ideal same-level projectile, H = u²sin²θ/(2g) and R = u²sin(2θ)/g.
Set H = R, cancel u²/g, and obtain sin²θ/2 = sin(2θ) = 2sinθ cosθ.
For a nonzero launch angle, sinθ = 4cosθ, so tanθ = 4.

numericals.note: The result relies on ideal flight with equal launch and landing heights.

numericals.question: A landing jet has speed 100 m/s and can decelerate uniformly at 5.0 m/s². Determine its minimum stopping time and distance. Could it stop on a runway 0.8 km long?

steps.text: From v = u + at: 0 = 100 − 5t, so stopping time t = 20 s.
Use v² = u² + 2as: 0 = 100² + 2(−5)s.
Minimum stopping distance s = 10000/10 = 1000 m = 1.0 km.
No; 800 m is 200 m shorter than the calculated 1000 m required.

numericals.answer: 20 s; 1000 m; cannot stop within an 800 m runway.
numericals.sourceAnswer: 20 s; cannot; runway at least 1 km
numericals.note: Uses the textbook's stated uniform braking deceleration, not additional reverse thrust.

numericals.question: An ideal projectile is launched at 21.8 m/s at 35° above horizontal and lands at its launch level. Calculate (a) flight time, (b) maximum height, and (c) horizontal displacement. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
numericals.given: u = 21.8 m/s; θ = 35°; g = 9.8 m/s²; same-level landing.

steps.text: Vertical launch speed: uᵧ = u sinθ = 21.8 sin35° ≈ 12.50 m/s.
Time of flight: T = 2uᵧ/g = 2(21.8 sin35°)/9.8 ≈ 2.55 s.
Maximum height relationship: H = uᵧ²/(2g).
Range relationship: R = (u cosθ)T = u²sin(2θ)/g.

numericals.note: Retain sensible rounding; equivalent correct substitutions receive credit.

numericals.question: A projectile is launched horizontally from a cliff 45.2 m high and lands 17.6 m from the base. Find its launch speed, neglecting air resistance. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
numericals.given: h = 45.2 m; horizontal displacement x = 17.6 m; initial vertical speed = 0; g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.text: Vertical fall: h = ½gt², so t = √(2h/g).
Horizontal motion has constant vₓ, so vₓ = x/t.
vₓ = 17.6/3.04 ≈ 5.79 m/s (approximately 5.8 m/s).

numericals.note: The height and horizontal displacement refer to the same flight; do not use equal-height angled-range shortcuts.

numericals.question: Two equal-mass carts move toward one another on a level low-friction track. Cart 1 travels right at 2 m/s and cart 2 left at 1 m/s. They collide and roll together. Find their common final velocity.
numericals.given: m₁ = m₂ = m; u₁ = +2 m/s; u₂ = −1 m/s; carts stick together.

steps.text: Choose rightward positive; use isolated-system momentum conservation.
Before: p = m(+2) + m(−1) = m.
After: p = (2m)v, so 2mv = m.
v = +0.50 m/s: the joined carts move rightward.

numericals.note: Formative P-11-B-11. Useful teaching problem; not included as a standalone summative paper question.

numericals.question: A 0.5 kg ball moving right at +4 m/s collides elastically head-on with a stationary 3.5 kg ball. Find the two final velocities.
numericals.given: m₁ = 0.5 kg; m₂ = 3.5 kg; u₁ = +4 m/s; u₂ = 0; isolated head-on elastic collision.

steps.text: Use both total momentum and kinetic-energy conservation for a head-on elastic collision.
v₁ = [(m₁−m₂)u₁ + 2m₂u₂]/(m₁+m₂).
v₂ = [2m₁u₁ + (m₂−m₁)u₂]/(m₁+m₂).
Check: initial p=2.0 kg·m/s; final p=(0.5)(−3)+(3.5)(1)=2.0 kg·m/s. Total kinetic energy before and after is 4.0 J.

numericals.note: A negative velocity indicates rebound relative to the chosen rightward-positive axis.

numericals.question: A 17.5 g bullet leaves an 8.0 kg gun at 582 m/s after moving through a 75.0 cm barrel. Assuming uniform acceleration from rest, calculate (a) barrel-travel time, (b) average barrel force, (c) impulse, and (d) bullet momentum at exit.
numericals.given: m = 0.0175 kg; v = 582 m/s; u = 0; barrel length s = 0.750 m; gun mass given but not required for the four requested quantities.

steps.text: Average barrel force on bullet F = ma = (0.0175)(225816) ≈ 3950 N.
Bullet momentum at exit p = mv = (0.0175)(582) ≈ 10.2 kg·m/s.

numericals.sourceAnswer: 0.00258 s; 3950 N; 10.2 N·s; 10.2 kg·m/s (printed source uses corresponding momentum units)
numericals.note: Supplementary formative/cross-topic recoil and impulse calculation; omitted from the summative practice paper. Source gun mass is unnecessary for parts a–d; do not invent a fifth part.
